chapter_text:
CHAPTER 10 - FORCE AND MOTION

Introduction

In our daily life we constantly push, pull, lift, throw, kick and stop objects. Every one of these actions is an example of a FORCE acting on a body. A football starts moving only when it is kicked; a moving car stops only when the brakes are applied; a rubber ball changes shape when squeezed. In this chapter we study what a force is, how forces change the state of motion of bodies, and the three famous laws of motion given by Sir Isaac Newton (1642-1727). We also study momentum, the conservation of momentum, and friction - a force we meet everywhere.

10.1 FORCE AND ITS EFFECTS

A FORCE is a push or a pull that one body exerts on another. Force is a vector quantity - it has both magnitude and direction. Its SI unit is the newton (N).

A force acting on a body can produce the following effects:
 1. It can set a stationary body into motion (a kick starts a ball moving).
 2. It can stop or slow down a moving body (brakes stop a car).
 3. It can change the speed of a moving body (pressing the accelerator).
 4. It can change the direction of motion of a body (a batsman deflects a ball).
 5. It can change the shape and size of a body (squeezing a sponge, stretching a spring).

Effects 1 to 4 are changes in the STATE OF MOTION; effect 5 is a change in shape (deformation).

Balanced and unbalanced forces.
Usually more than one force acts on a body at the same time. If the forces acting on a body cancel out - their resultant (net force) is zero - the forces are said to be BALANCED. Balanced forces do NOT change the state of motion of a body: a book lying on a table has the downward pull of gravity balanced by the upward push of the table, so it stays at rest. In a tug of war, when both teams pull equally the rope does not move - the forces are balanced. Balanced forces can, however, change the shape of a body (the rope becomes taut).

If the forces acting on a body do NOT cancel - the net force is non-zero - the forces are UNBALANCED. Unbalanced forces change the state of motion: they make a body start moving, speed up, slow down, stop, or change direction. When one tug-of-war team pulls harder, the rope (and the other team) moves in that direction. So it is the UNBALANCED force that is responsible for acceleration.

10.2 NEWTON'S FIRST LAW OF MOTION (LAW OF INERTIA)

Newton's First Law states: A body continues in its state of rest, or of uniform motion in a straight line, unless it is acted upon by an external unbalanced force.

This means a body left to itself will not change its state of motion on its own. A body at rest stays at rest; a body moving with constant velocity keeps moving with the same speed in the same straight line - until some outside unbalanced force changes it.

INERTIA. The natural tendency of a body to resist any change in its state of rest or of uniform motion is called INERTIA. Because the first law expresses this property, it is also called the LAW OF INERTIA. A body has no force of its own to change its state; it simply 'wants' to keep doing what it is already doing.

Inertia and mass. The inertia of a body depends on its MASS. A heavier body has more inertia than a lighter body. It is easy to push a bicycle but very hard to push a loaded truck, because the truck has far greater mass and hence far greater inertia. Thus MASS is a measure of inertia.

Types of inertia:
 (a) Inertia of rest - a body at rest resists being moved. When a bus starts suddenly, passengers fall backward, because the lower body moves with the bus but the upper body tends to stay at rest. Dust falls off a carpet when it is beaten, because the carpet moves while the dust stays at rest.
 (b) Inertia of motion - a moving body resists being stopped. When a moving bus stops suddenly, passengers lurch forward, because their bodies tend to keep moving. An athlete runs some distance before a long jump so that the inertia of motion carries the body farther.
 (c) Inertia of direction - a body resists a change in its direction of motion. When a car takes a sharp turn, passengers are pushed to the outer side, because the body tends to keep moving in a straight line. Mud flies off tangentially from the wheels of a moving vehicle.

10.3 MOMENTUM

A heavy truck moving slowly and a light bullet moving fast can both cause great damage. Clearly the effect of a moving body depends on BOTH its mass and its velocity. This combined quantity is called MOMENTUM.

The momentum (p) of a body is the product of its mass (m) and its velocity (v):

   p = m v

Momentum is a vector quantity; its direction is the same as the direction of the velocity. The SI unit of momentum is the kilogram metre per second (kg m/s). A large momentum means the body is hard to stop. A loaded truck at 10 m/s has enormous momentum; a cricket ball at the same speed has very little. This is why a small bullet (small mass, very high velocity) and a slow lorry (large mass, small velocity) can both carry large momentum.

10.4 NEWTON'S SECOND LAW OF MOTION

Newton's Second Law states: The rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the applied unbalanced force, and the change takes place in the direction of the force.

Let a force F act on a body of mass m for time t, changing its velocity from u to v. Initial momentum = m u; final momentum = m v.
Change in momentum = m v - m u = m (v - u).
Rate of change of momentum = m (v - u) / t.
But (v - u) / t = a, the acceleration. So rate of change of momentum = m a.
By the law, F is proportional to m a, i.e. F = k m a. Choosing units so that k = 1, we get the famous equation:

   F = m a

So force = mass x acceleration. We can also write F = (m v - m u) / t = rate of change of momentum.

The unit of force - the newton. One NEWTON is the force that gives a mass of 1 kilogram an acceleration of 1 metre per second squared:
   1 N = 1 kg x 1 m/s^2 = 1 kg m/s^2.

The second law explains many everyday observations. A cricketer draws his hands back while catching a fast ball: this increases the time t over which the ball's momentum is reduced to zero, so the rate of change of momentum (and hence the force on his hands) is smaller. The same idea explains why we bend our knees on landing, why packaging uses soft material, and why vehicles have crumple zones and air bags.

10.5 NEWTON'S THIRD LAW OF MOTION

Newton's Third Law states: To every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.

Whenever one body exerts a force (action) on a second body, the second body exerts an equal force in the opposite direction (reaction) on the first. Action and reaction are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, and act on DIFFERENT bodies (so they never cancel each other).

Examples:
 - When you walk, your foot pushes the ground backward (action); the ground pushes you forward (reaction).
 - A swimmer pushes the water backward; the water pushes the swimmer forward.
 - A gun recoils backward when a bullet is fired forward.
 - The hot gases of a rocket are pushed downward; the reaction pushes the rocket upward.
 - A boat moves backward when a person jumps from it to the shore.

10.6 CONSERVATION OF MOMENTUM

The law of conservation of momentum states: In the absence of an external unbalanced force, the total momentum of a system of bodies remains constant. In other words, the total momentum before an interaction equals the total momentum after it.

Derivation from the third law. Consider two bodies A and B of masses m1 and m2 moving with velocities u1 and u2 (u1 > u2) along the same line. They collide for a time t and then move with velocities v1 and v2.
During the collision, A exerts a force F_AB on B and, by the third law, B exerts an equal and opposite force F_BA = -F_AB on A.
Force on B = m2 (v2 - u2)/t ; force on A = m1 (v1 - u1)/t.
Since F_BA = -F_AB:
   m1 (v1 - u1)/t = -m2 (v2 - u2)/t
Cancelling t and rearranging:
   m1 u1 + m2 u2 = m1 v1 + m2 v2.
That is, total momentum before collision = total momentum after collision.

Applications:
 (a) Recoil of a gun. Before firing, gun + bullet are at rest, so total momentum = 0. After firing, the bullet (mass m, velocity v) moves forward with momentum m v; to keep the total at zero the gun (mass M) must move backward with velocity V such that M V = m v, i.e. V = m v / M. Because M is large, the recoil velocity V is small.
 (b) Rocket propulsion. Hot gases are ejected downward with high momentum; an equal and opposite momentum is given to the rocket, pushing it upward. The rocket keeps the total momentum of (rocket + gases) conserved.
 (c) Collisions. In games like carrom and billiards, and in vehicle collisions, the total momentum of the colliding bodies is conserved.

10.7 FRICTION

FRICTION is the force that opposes the relative motion (or tendency of motion) between two surfaces in contact. It always acts along the surfaces and in the direction OPPOSITE to the motion. Friction arises because no surface is perfectly smooth - on a microscopic scale every surface has tiny bumps and hollows that interlock, and overcoming this interlocking needs force.

Types of friction:
 (a) Static friction - the friction acting between two surfaces at rest relative to each other; it prevents an object from starting to move. It adjusts itself up to a maximum value (limiting friction).
 (b) Kinetic (sliding) friction - the friction acting when one surface slides over another. It is slightly less than the maximum static friction.
 (c) Rolling friction - the friction when a body rolls over a surface. Rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction; that is why wheels and ball bearings are used.

Advantages of friction:
 - We can walk only because of friction between our feet and the ground (on ice, with little friction, we slip).
 - Vehicles can move and stop because of friction between tyres and road and in the brakes.
 - We can write with a pen or pencil, hold objects, light a matchstick, and tie a knot only because of friction.

Disadvantages of friction:
 - Friction wears out the soles of shoes, tyres, and machine parts.
 - Friction produces heat and wastes useful energy in machines, lowering their efficiency.
 - Friction reduces the speed of moving parts and machines.

Methods to reduce friction:
 - Polishing surfaces to make them smoother.
 - Using lubricants such as oil and grease between moving parts.
 - Using ball bearings to convert sliding friction into rolling friction.
 - Streamlining the shape of vehicles, aeroplanes and ships to reduce friction with air and water.

WORKED NUMERICAL EXAMPLES

Example 1. A force of 20 N acts on a body of mass 4 kg. Find the acceleration.
Solution: a = F / m = 20 / 4 = 5 m/s^2.

Example 2. A car of mass 1000 kg moving at 20 m/s is brought to rest in 5 s. Find the braking force.
Solution: a = (v - u)/t = (0 - 20)/5 = -4 m/s^2. F = m a = 1000 x (-4) = -4000 N. The negative sign shows the force opposes the motion; magnitude 4000 N.

Example 3. Find the momentum of a 2 kg ball moving at 3 m/s.
Solution: p = m v = 2 x 3 = 6 kg m/s.

Example 4. A bullet of mass 0.02 kg is fired with a velocity of 200 m/s from a gun of mass 4 kg. Find the recoil velocity of the gun.
Solution: By conservation of momentum, M V = m v, so V = m v / M = (0.02 x 200)/4 = 4/4 = 1 m/s (backward).

SUMMARY

- A force is a push or a pull; it can change the state of motion or the shape of a body. The SI unit of force is the newton (N).
- Balanced forces (net force zero) do not change the state of motion; unbalanced forces (net force non-zero) do.
- Newton's First Law (law of inertia): a body keeps its state of rest or uniform motion unless an unbalanced force acts on it. Inertia is the resistance to change of state; mass measures inertia. Three types: of rest, of motion, of direction.
- Momentum p = m v (unit kg m/s) is a vector; it measures the 'quantity of motion'.
- Newton's Second Law: force = rate of change of momentum = m a. One newton = 1 kg m/s^2.
- Newton's Third Law: every action has an equal and opposite reaction, acting on different bodies.
- Conservation of momentum: total momentum of an isolated system is constant; m1 u1 + m2 u2 = m1 v1 + m2 v2. It explains gun recoil, rocket propulsion and collisions.
- Friction opposes relative motion; it is static, kinetic or rolling. It is useful (walking, gripping, braking) but also wastes energy and wears parts. It is reduced by polishing, lubricants, ball bearings and streamlining.

chapter_summary.title: Force and Motion - Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This NIOS Class 10 Science & Technology (212) summary for Lesson 10 explains what a force is and how balanced and unbalanced forces affect motion. It develops Newton's three laws of motion, the idea of inertia and momentum, the conservation of momentum, and the everyday force of friction.

sections.heading: Force, its effects and balanced/unbalanced forces
bullets: A force is a push or a pull exerted by one body on another; it is a vector quantity measured in newtons (N).
A force can start motion, stop motion, change speed, change direction, or change the shape and size of a body.
Balanced forces have zero resultant and do not change the state of motion; unbalanced forces have a non-zero resultant and produce acceleration.

sections.heading: Newton's First Law and inertia
bullets: Newton's First Law: a body stays at rest or in uniform straight-line motion unless an external unbalanced force acts on it.
Inertia is the tendency of a body to resist any change in its state of rest or uniform motion; the law is also called the law of inertia.
Inertia depends on mass: a heavier body has greater inertia. The three types are inertia of rest, of motion and of direction.

sections.heading: Momentum
bullets: Momentum p = m v is the product of mass and velocity and measures the 'quantity of motion' of a body.
Momentum is a vector with the same direction as velocity; its SI unit is the kilogram metre per second (kg m/s).
A light fast bullet and a heavy slow truck can both have large momentum, so both are hard to stop.

sections.heading: Newton's Second Law and the newton
bullets: Newton's Second Law: the rate of change of momentum is proportional to the applied force and is in the direction of the force.
From m(v-u)/t = m a we obtain F = m a; force can also be written as the rate of change of momentum (mv - mu)/t.
One newton is the force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s^2, i.e. 1 N = 1 kg m/s^2.

sections.heading: Third law, conservation of momentum and friction
bullets: Newton's Third Law: to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction; the two forces act on different bodies.
Conservation of momentum: m1 u1 + m2 u2 = m1 v1 + m2 v2 for an isolated system; it explains gun recoil and rocket propulsion.
Friction opposes relative motion (static, kinetic, rolling); it is useful for walking and braking but wastes energy and is reduced by lubricants and ball bearings.

key_takeaways: A force is a push or a pull that can change the state of motion or the shape of a body; its SI unit is the newton.
Balanced forces leave the state of motion unchanged; only an unbalanced (net) force produces acceleration.
Newton's First Law (law of inertia): bodies resist changes to rest or uniform motion, and mass measures this inertia.
Momentum p = m v (unit kg m/s) is a vector measuring the quantity of motion.
Newton's Second Law gives F = m a = rate of change of momentum; 1 N = 1 kg m/s^2.
Newton's Third Law and conservation of momentum (m1 u1 + m2 u2 = m1 v1 + m2 v2) explain recoil, rockets and collisions.
Friction opposes relative motion - it is static, kinetic or rolling - and is reduced by polishing, lubricants, ball bearings and streamlining.

glossary.definition: A push or a pull that one body exerts on another; a vector quantity measured in newtons (N) that can change a body's motion or shape.
Forces acting on a body whose resultant (net force) is zero; they do not change the body's state of motion.
A non-zero net force acting on a body; it changes the body's state of motion by producing acceleration.
A body continues at rest or in uniform straight-line motion unless acted upon by an external unbalanced force.
The natural tendency of a body to resist any change in its state of rest or of uniform motion; it depends on mass.
The tendency of a body at rest to remain at rest, e.g. passengers fall backward when a bus starts suddenly.
The tendency of a moving body to keep moving, e.g. passengers lurch forward when a bus stops suddenly.
The product of mass and velocity, p = m v; a vector quantity with SI unit kilogram metre per second (kg m/s).
The rate of change of momentum of a body is proportional to the applied force and is in its direction, giving F = m a.
The SI unit of force; one newton gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s^2, so 1 N = 1 kg m/s^2.
To every action there is an equal and opposite reaction; the two forces act on different bodies.
In the absence of an external force, the total momentum of a system stays constant: m1 u1 + m2 u2 = m1 v1 + m2 v2.
The force that opposes relative motion between two surfaces in contact; it acts along the surfaces opposite to motion.
The friction when a body rolls over a surface; much smaller than sliding friction, which is why wheels and ball bearings are used.
A substance such as oil or grease applied between moving parts to reduce friction and wear.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Force and Motion (NIOS Official)
worksheet.instructions: This is the NIOS Secondary Science & Technology (212) worksheet for Lesson 10. Attempt all questions. Take g = 10 m/s^2 where needed and show all steps in numerical problems.

questions.question: Define force and list any four effects a force can produce on a body.
questions.answer:
A force is a push or a pull that one body exerts on another. It is a vector quantity (has magnitude and direction) and is measured in newtons (N).
Four effects of a force:
1. It can set a stationary body into motion.
2. It can stop or slow down a moving body.
3. It can change the speed or the direction of a moving body.
4. It can change the shape and size of a body (e.g. squeezing a sponge).
questions.explanation: Definition plus any four standard effects.

questions.question: State Newton's First Law of Motion and explain what is meant by inertia.
questions.answer:
Newton's First Law: A body continues in its state of rest, or of uniform motion in a straight line, unless acted upon by an external unbalanced force.
Inertia is the natural tendency of a body to resist any change in its state of rest or of uniform motion. Because the first law describes this property, it is also called the law of inertia. The inertia of a body depends on its mass - a heavier body has greater inertia.
questions.explanation: Statement of the law plus the meaning of inertia and its link to mass.

questions.question: Explain the three types of inertia with one example each.
questions.answer:
(a) Inertia of rest: a body at rest resists being moved. Example: when a bus starts suddenly, passengers fall backward.
(b) Inertia of motion: a moving body resists being stopped. Example: when a moving bus stops suddenly, passengers lurch forward.
(c) Inertia of direction: a body resists a change in its direction of motion. Example: when a car turns sharply, passengers are pushed to the outer side.
questions.explanation: Name each type and give a correct everyday example.

questions.question: Define momentum, give its formula and SI unit, and calculate the momentum of a 5 kg body moving at 4 m/s.
questions.answer:
Momentum is the product of the mass and velocity of a body. It is a vector quantity.
Formula: p = m v.
SI unit: kilogram metre per second (kg m/s).
Calculation: p = m v = 5 kg x 4 m/s = 20 kg m/s, directed along the velocity.
questions.explanation: Definition, formula, unit and a one-step calculation.

questions.question: State Newton's Second Law of Motion and derive the relation F = m a.
questions.answer:
Newton's Second Law: The rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the applied unbalanced force and takes place in the direction of the force.
Derivation: Let a force F act on a body of mass m for time t, changing its velocity from u to v.
Initial momentum = m u; final momentum = m v.
Change in momentum = m v - m u = m (v - u).
Rate of change of momentum = m (v - u) / t.
Since (v - u)/t = a (acceleration), rate of change of momentum = m a.
By the law, F is proportional to m a, so F = k m a. Choosing SI units so that k = 1 gives F = m a.
Thus force = mass x acceleration.
questions.explanation: State the law and carry out the standard derivation to F = m a.

questions.question: A force of 30 N acts on a body of mass 6 kg. Calculate the acceleration produced. If the same force acts for 4 s on a body initially at rest, find its final velocity.
questions.answer:
Acceleration: a = F / m = 30 / 6 = 5 m/s^2.
Final velocity: using v = u + a t with u = 0, a = 5 m/s^2, t = 4 s:
v = 0 + 5 x 4 = 20 m/s.
So the acceleration is 5 m/s^2 and the final velocity is 20 m/s.
questions.explanation: Apply F = m a then v = u + a t.

questions.question: State Newton's Third Law of Motion. Give two examples and explain why action and reaction do not cancel each other.
questions.answer:
Newton's Third Law: To every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.
Examples: (1) When you walk, your foot pushes the ground backward and the ground pushes you forward. (2) A gun recoils backward when a bullet is fired forward.
Action and reaction do not cancel because they act on TWO DIFFERENT bodies (e.g. one on the foot, the other on the ground). Two forces can cancel only when they act on the same body, which is never the case for an action-reaction pair.
questions.explanation: Statement, two examples, and the key point that the forces act on different bodies.

questions.question: A bullet of mass 0.05 kg is fired with a velocity of 240 m/s from a gun of mass 6 kg. Using conservation of momentum, find the recoil velocity of the gun.
questions.answer:
Before firing the gun and bullet are at rest, so total momentum = 0.
By conservation of momentum, total momentum after firing is also 0:
m (bullet) x v (bullet) + M (gun) x V (gun) = 0
(0.05 x 240) + (6 x V) = 0
12 + 6 V = 0
V = -12 / 6 = -2 m/s.
The negative sign shows the gun moves opposite to the bullet. So the recoil velocity of the gun is 2 m/s backward.
questions.explanation: Set total momentum before = after = 0 and solve for the gun's velocity.

questions.question: Distinguish between static, kinetic and rolling friction, and state which is the smallest.
questions.answer:
Static friction acts between two surfaces that are at rest relative to each other and prevents motion from starting; it adjusts up to a maximum (limiting) value.
Kinetic (sliding) friction acts when one surface slides over another; it is slightly less than the maximum static friction.
Rolling friction acts when a body rolls over a surface.
Rolling friction is the SMALLEST of the three, which is why wheels and ball bearings are used to make movement easier.
questions.explanation: Define each type and identify rolling friction as smallest.

questions.question: Give two advantages and two disadvantages of friction, and state two methods of reducing it.
questions.answer:
Advantages: (1) Friction lets us walk without slipping. (2) Friction lets vehicles move and stop (tyres grip the road; brakes work). Other examples: writing, gripping objects.
Disadvantages: (1) Friction wears out shoe soles, tyres and machine parts. (2) Friction produces heat and wastes energy in machines, lowering their efficiency.
Methods of reducing friction: (1) Using lubricants such as oil and grease. (2) Using ball bearings to convert sliding friction into rolling friction. (Polishing surfaces and streamlining also help.)
questions.explanation: Two advantages, two disadvantages and two reduction methods.

questions.question: Define force and give its SI unit.
questions.answer: A force is a push or a pull that one body exerts on another. It is a vector quantity having both magnitude and direction. Its SI unit is the newton (N).
questions.explanation: Definition plus SI unit.

questions.question: List five effects that a force can produce on a body.
questions.answer: (1) It can set a stationary body into motion. (2) It can stop or slow down a moving body. (3) It can change the speed of a moving body. (4) It can change the direction of motion. (5) It can change the shape and size of a body.
questions.explanation: Any five standard effects of force.

questions.question: Distinguish between balanced and unbalanced forces with one example each.
questions.answer:
Balanced forces: their resultant (net force) is zero, so they do not change the state of motion. Example: a book resting on a table - weight down balanced by the table's push up.
Unbalanced forces: their resultant is non-zero, so they change the state of motion (cause acceleration). Example: pushing a stationary cart so that it starts moving.
questions.explanation: Net force zero vs non-zero, with examples.

questions.question: Why is force called a vector quantity?
questions.answer: Force is called a vector quantity because it has both magnitude (how strong the push or pull is) and direction (which way it acts). To describe a force completely we must state both. Vectors also add according to the rules of vector addition.
questions.explanation: Both magnitude and direction are needed.

questions.question: State Newton's First Law of Motion.
questions.answer: Newton's First Law: A body continues in its state of rest, or of uniform motion in a straight line, unless it is acted upon by an external unbalanced force.
questions.explanation: Standard statement of the first law.

questions.question: Explain the meaning of inertia and how it depends on mass.
questions.answer:
Inertia is the natural tendency of a body to resist any change in its state of rest or of uniform motion. A body cannot change its own state of motion; an external force is needed.
Inertia depends on mass: the greater the mass, the greater the inertia. That is why it is easy to push a bicycle but very hard to push a loaded truck. Mass is therefore a measure of inertia.
questions.explanation: Definition and the role of mass.

questions.question: Why is it dangerous to stand in a moving bus and why should one hold the handrail?
questions.answer: When the bus suddenly starts, stops or turns, the lower body moves with the bus but the upper body tends to keep its earlier state of motion because of inertia. A standing passenger can therefore be thrown backward (sudden start), forward (sudden stop) or sideways (turn) and may fall. Holding the handrail supplies the external force needed to keep the whole body moving with the bus, preventing a fall.
questions.explanation: Inertia of rest/motion/direction acting on the passenger.

questions.question: Explain why dust is removed when a carpet is beaten with a stick.
questions.answer: When the carpet is struck, the carpet suddenly moves but the dust particles in it tend to stay at rest because of their inertia of rest. As the carpet moves away from the dust, the dust particles are left behind and fall down under gravity. Thus beating the carpet removes the dust.
questions.explanation: Inertia of rest of the dust particles.

questions.question: Why does an athlete run a short distance before taking a long jump?
questions.answer: By running before the jump the athlete gains velocity and hence momentum. At take-off the body already has inertia of motion, which carries it forward through the air and lets it cover a greater horizontal distance than a standing jump. The running build-up therefore increases the length of the jump.
questions.explanation: Inertia of motion gained by running.

questions.question: Define momentum and calculate the momentum of a 10 kg body moving at 6 m/s.
questions.answer:
Momentum is the product of the mass and velocity of a body, p = m v. It is a vector with SI unit kg m/s.
Calculation: p = m v = 10 kg x 6 m/s = 60 kg m/s in the direction of motion.
questions.explanation: Definition plus one-step calculation.

questions.question: A truck of mass 2000 kg moves at 15 m/s. Find its momentum.
questions.answer: Momentum p = m v = 2000 kg x 15 m/s = 30000 kg m/s, directed along the truck's motion. Its large value shows the truck is very hard to stop.
questions.explanation: p = m v with given data.

questions.question: A light bullet and a heavy lorry can both be dangerous. Explain using momentum.
questions.answer: The damage a moving body can cause depends on its momentum, p = m v. A bullet has very small mass but extremely high velocity, so its momentum is large. A lorry has a large mass even at modest velocity, so its momentum is also large. Because both have large momentum, both are hard to stop and can cause serious damage on impact.
questions.explanation: Momentum depends on both mass and velocity.

questions.question: A body of mass 4 kg has a momentum of 28 kg m/s. Find its velocity.
questions.answer: Using p = m v, velocity v = p / m = 28 / 4 = 7 m/s. The body moves at 7 m/s in the direction of its momentum.
questions.explanation: Rearrange p = m v to v = p/m.

questions.question: State Newton's Second Law of Motion.
questions.answer: Newton's Second Law: The rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the applied unbalanced force and takes place in the direction of the force. This leads to F = m a.
questions.explanation: Statement of the second law.

questions.question: A force of 40 N acts on a body of mass 8 kg. Find the acceleration produced.
questions.answer: Acceleration a = F / m = 40 N / 8 kg = 5 m/s^2 in the direction of the force.
questions.explanation: Apply a = F/m.

questions.question: A car of mass 1200 kg accelerates from rest to 20 m/s in 8 s. Find the force acting on it.
questions.answer:
Acceleration a = (v - u)/t = (20 - 0)/8 = 2.5 m/s^2.
Force F = m a = 1200 x 2.5 = 3000 N.
So a force of 3000 N acts on the car.
questions.explanation: Find a, then F = m a.

questions.question: A 5 kg body moving at 12 m/s is stopped in 3 s. Find the stopping force.
questions.answer:
Acceleration a = (v - u)/t = (0 - 12)/3 = -4 m/s^2.
Force F = m a = 5 x (-4) = -20 N.
The negative sign shows the force opposes the motion; its magnitude is 20 N.
questions.explanation: Deceleration then F = m a.

questions.question: Why does a cricketer move his hands backward while catching a fast ball?
questions.answer: By drawing the hands back, the cricketer increases the time t over which the ball's momentum is reduced to zero. Since force equals the rate of change of momentum (F = change in momentum / time), increasing the time reduces the force on the hands. This lessens the impact and prevents injury.
questions.explanation: Increasing time lowers the rate of change of momentum.

questions.question: Define one newton of force.
questions.answer: One newton is the force that gives a mass of 1 kilogram an acceleration of 1 metre per second squared. In base units, 1 N = 1 kg m/s^2.
questions.explanation: Definition of the newton.

questions.question: The momentum of a body changes from 10 kg m/s to 30 kg m/s in 4 s. Find the force acting on it.
questions.answer:
Change in momentum = 30 - 10 = 20 kg m/s.
Force = rate of change of momentum = change in momentum / time = 20 / 4 = 5 N.
So a force of 5 N acts on the body.
questions.explanation: F = change in momentum / time.

questions.question: A force of 8 N acts on a body for 5 s. Find the change in its momentum.
questions.answer: Force = change in momentum / time, so change in momentum = F x t = 8 N x 5 s = 40 kg m/s. (This product F t is called the impulse.)
questions.explanation: Change in momentum = F t.

questions.question: State Newton's Third Law of Motion with one example.
questions.answer: Newton's Third Law: To every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. Example: when you walk, your foot pushes the ground backward (action) and the ground pushes you forward (reaction).
questions.explanation: Statement plus an example.

questions.question: Why do action and reaction forces not cancel each other?
questions.answer: Action and reaction are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, but they act on TWO DIFFERENT bodies - for example, one on the foot and the other on the ground. Two forces can cancel (produce no net effect) only when they act on the same body. Since action and reaction never act on the same body, they cannot cancel each other.
questions.explanation: They act on different bodies.

questions.question: State the law of conservation of momentum.
questions.answer: The law of conservation of momentum states that in the absence of an external unbalanced force, the total momentum of a system of bodies remains constant; that is, the total momentum before an interaction equals the total momentum after it.
questions.explanation: Standard statement.

questions.question: Explain how a rocket moves up using Newton's Third Law.
questions.answer: A rocket burns fuel and ejects hot gases downward at high speed (action). By Newton's Third Law, the gases push the rocket upward with an equal and opposite force (reaction). The continuous backward ejection of gas gives the rocket a forward (upward) thrust, so it rises. The total momentum of the rocket and the ejected gases stays conserved.
questions.explanation: Action on gases, reaction on rocket.

questions.question: A bullet of mass 0.04 kg is fired at 100 m/s from a 4 kg gun. Find the recoil velocity of the gun.
questions.answer:
Before firing, total momentum = 0. By conservation of momentum:
m(bullet) x v(bullet) + M(gun) x V(gun) = 0
(0.04 x 100) + (4 x V) = 0
4 + 4 V = 0
V = -1 m/s.
The gun recoils at 1 m/s in the direction opposite to the bullet.
questions.explanation: Set total momentum before = after = 0.

questions.question: What is friction? In which direction does it act?
questions.answer: Friction is the force that opposes the relative motion (or tendency of motion) between two surfaces in contact. It acts along the surfaces in the direction OPPOSITE to the motion or attempted motion of the body.
questions.explanation: Definition and direction.

questions.question: Name the three types of friction and state which is the largest and which is the smallest.
questions.answer:
The three types are static friction, kinetic (sliding) friction and rolling friction.
Static friction (its limiting value) is the largest; kinetic friction is slightly less; rolling friction is the smallest of the three. This is why rolling (wheels, ball bearings) is preferred to sliding.
questions.explanation: Static (limiting) largest, rolling smallest.

questions.question: Friction is both a friend and a foe. Justify this statement.
questions.answer:
Friction is a friend because it is essential for many activities: we can walk, grip objects, write with a pen, and vehicles can move and brake only because of friction. Without it, surfaces would be like ice and nothing could be held or driven.
Friction is a foe because it wears out shoe soles, tyres and machine parts, produces heat, and wastes useful energy, lowering the efficiency of machines. So friction is both useful and harmful.
questions.explanation: Advantages vs disadvantages.

questions.question: State four methods of reducing friction.
questions.answer: (1) Polishing the surfaces to make them smoother. (2) Using lubricants such as oil and grease between moving parts. (3) Using ball bearings to convert sliding friction into rolling friction. (4) Streamlining the shape of vehicles, aircraft and ships to reduce friction with air or water.
questions.explanation: Any four standard methods.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A wooden box lies on the floor. Two children push it from opposite sides. Child A pushes with 30 N to the right and child B pushes with 30 N to the left. Later child A pushes with 40 N to the right while child B still pushes 30 N to the left.

(i) In the first case, what is the net force on the box?
(ii) Are the forces balanced or unbalanced in the first case?
(iii) Does the box move in the first case? Why?
(iv) In the second case, find the net force and its direction.
questions.answer:
(i) Net force = 30 N - 30 N = 0 N (the forces act in opposite directions and are equal).
(ii) The forces are balanced because the resultant is zero.
(iii) The box does not move, because balanced forces do not change the state of motion - there is no unbalanced force to cause acceleration.
(iv) Net force = 40 N - 30 N = 10 N directed to the right (the direction of the larger force). This unbalanced force makes the box move to the right.
questions.explanation: Balanced forces give no motion; unbalanced net force gives motion.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A passenger is standing in a bus. The driver suddenly applies the brakes and the bus stops quickly. The passenger lurches forward and almost falls.

(i) Which law of motion explains this?
(ii) Name the property of the body responsible.
(iii) Which type of inertia is involved?
(iv) Suggest one way the passenger can avoid falling.
questions.answer:
(i) Newton's First Law of Motion (the law of inertia) explains it.
(ii) The property is inertia - the tendency of the body to resist a change in its state of motion.
(iii) Inertia of motion is involved: the passenger's body was moving with the bus and tends to keep moving forward when the bus stops.
(iv) The passenger should hold a handrail or strap firmly, which supplies the external force needed to stop the upper body along with the bus and prevents a fall.
questions.explanation: Sudden stop -> inertia of motion -> body continues forward.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Momentum is the product of mass and velocity, p = m v, with unit kg m/s. A cricket ball of mass 0.16 kg moves at 25 m/s. A loaded lorry of mass 4000 kg moves at 2 m/s.

(i) Find the momentum of the cricket ball.
(ii) Find the momentum of the lorry.
(iii) Which has the greater momentum?
(iv) What does this tell us about stopping each body?
questions.answer:
(i) Ball: p = m v = 0.16 x 25 = 4 kg m/s.
(ii) Lorry: p = m v = 4000 x 2 = 8000 kg m/s.
(iii) The lorry has the far greater momentum (8000 kg m/s vs 4 kg m/s).
(iv) The greater the momentum, the harder it is to stop the body. The lorry, with much larger momentum, needs a much larger force (or much longer time) to bring it to rest than the cricket ball.
questions.explanation: p = m v for each; larger momentum is harder to stop.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Newton's Second Law gives F = m a. A motorcycle of mass 150 kg (with rider) starts from rest and reaches 12 m/s in 6 s along a straight road.

(i) Find the acceleration of the motorcycle.
(ii) Find the force acting on it.
(iii) If the same force acted on a 300 kg vehicle, what would its acceleration be?
(iv) What does this show about the relation between mass and acceleration for a fixed force?
questions.answer:
(i) a = (v - u)/t = (12 - 0)/6 = 2 m/s^2.
(ii) F = m a = 150 x 2 = 300 N.
(iii) For the 300 kg vehicle, a = F/m = 300/300 = 1 m/s^2.
(iv) For a fixed force, acceleration is inversely proportional to mass: doubling the mass (150 kg to 300 kg) halves the acceleration (2 m/s^2 to 1 m/s^2).
questions.explanation: Find a, then F = m a; a = F/m for the heavier body.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Force can be expressed as the rate of change of momentum, F = (m v - m u)/t. A ball of mass 0.5 kg moving at 8 m/s is stopped by a wall in 0.2 s.

(i) Find the initial momentum of the ball.
(ii) Find the change in momentum.
(iii) Find the force exerted by the wall on the ball.
(iv) If the ball were stopped in 0.4 s instead, how would the force change?
questions.answer:
(i) Initial momentum = m u = 0.5 x 8 = 4 kg m/s.
(ii) Final momentum = 0 (the ball stops). Change in momentum = 0 - 4 = -4 kg m/s (magnitude 4 kg m/s).
(iii) Force = change in momentum / time = 4 / 0.2 = 20 N (opposing the motion).
(iv) If the time is doubled to 0.4 s, force = 4 / 0.4 = 10 N. Doubling the stopping time halves the force - this is why increasing the time of impact reduces the force.
questions.explanation: F = change in momentum / time; longer time -> smaller force.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Conservation of momentum: for an isolated system the total momentum before = total momentum after. A gun of mass 5 kg fires a bullet of mass 0.05 kg with a velocity of 200 m/s.

(i) What is the total momentum of the system before firing?
(ii) Find the momentum of the bullet after firing.
(iii) Find the recoil velocity of the gun.
(iv) Why is the recoil velocity of the gun much smaller than the bullet's velocity?
questions.answer:
(i) Before firing, both gun and bullet are at rest, so total momentum = 0.
(ii) Momentum of bullet = m v = 0.05 x 200 = 10 kg m/s (forward).
(iii) By conservation, gun momentum = -10 kg m/s. Recoil velocity V = momentum / mass = 10 / 5 = 2 m/s backward.
(iv) The recoil velocity is small because the gun has a much larger mass than the bullet. Since the two momenta are equal in size (m v = M V), the larger mass M gives a much smaller velocity V.
questions.explanation: Total momentum stays 0; large gun mass -> small recoil speed.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Two trolleys collide and move together (a perfectly inelastic collision). Trolley A (mass 3 kg) moves at 4 m/s and hits a stationary trolley B (mass 1 kg). After the collision they stick together and move with a common velocity v.

(i) Write the total momentum before the collision.
(ii) Write the expression for the total momentum after the collision.
(iii) Find the common velocity v.
(iv) Which law did you use?
questions.answer:
(i) Before: total momentum = (3 x 4) + (1 x 0) = 12 kg m/s.
(ii) After: the combined mass is (3 + 1) = 4 kg moving at v, so total momentum = 4 v.
(iii) By conservation, 12 = 4 v, so v = 12 / 4 = 3 m/s.
(iv) The law of conservation of momentum (which follows from Newton's Third Law).
questions.explanation: Conserve momentum: m1 u1 + m2 u2 = (m1+m2) v.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Friction opposes relative motion between surfaces in contact. It can be static, kinetic or rolling. It is useful in some situations and harmful in others, and engineers use several methods to reduce it.

(i) Why is it hard to walk on a smooth icy road?
(ii) Name the type of friction that is smallest.
(iii) Give one harmful effect of friction in machines.
(iv) State two methods used to reduce friction.
questions.answer:
(i) On smooth ice there is very little friction between the feet and the surface. Without enough friction the feet cannot grip the ground, so they slip and walking is difficult.
(ii) Rolling friction is the smallest.
(iii) In machines friction wears out the moving parts and produces heat, wasting useful energy and lowering efficiency.
(iv) Two methods: (a) using lubricants such as oil and grease, and (b) using ball bearings to convert sliding friction into rolling friction. (Polishing and streamlining also help.)
questions.explanation: Friction's role in walking, its harm, and how to reduce it.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Inertia is the resistance of a body to a change in its state of motion. It appears in three forms - inertia of rest, of motion and of direction - in many everyday situations.

(i) A coin on a card over a glass falls into the glass when the card is flicked away. Which type of inertia is this?
(ii) Mud flies off the wheels of a moving cycle. Which type of inertia is this?
(iii) Why do we beat a dusty blanket with a stick?
(iv) Which physical quantity decides how much inertia a body has?
questions.answer:
(i) Inertia of rest: the coin, being at rest, tends to stay at rest as the card flies off, so it drops into the glass.
(ii) Inertia of direction: the mud tends to keep moving in a straight line and so flies off tangentially from the curved wheel.
(iii) Beating moves the blanket suddenly while the dust, by inertia of rest, stays in place and is left behind, so it falls off and the blanket is cleaned.
(iv) Mass decides the amount of inertia - a body with greater mass has greater inertia.
questions.explanation: Identify the type of inertia in each case; mass measures inertia.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Newton's Second Law (F = m a, and F = rate of change of momentum) explains many safety features in vehicles. A car of mass 1000 kg moving at 20 m/s is brought to rest. In a hard crash it stops in 0.5 s; with a crumple zone and air bag it stops in 2 s.

(i) Find the change in momentum of the car.
(ii) Find the force in the hard crash (0.5 s).
(iii) Find the force with the crumple zone (2 s).
(iv) Explain how crumple zones and air bags reduce injury.
questions.answer:
(i) Change in momentum = m v - m u = 1000 x 0 - 1000 x 20 = -20000 kg m/s (magnitude 20000 kg m/s).
(ii) Hard crash: force = change in momentum / time = 20000 / 0.5 = 40000 N.
(iii) With crumple zone: force = 20000 / 2 = 10000 N.
(iv) Crumple zones and air bags increase the time over which the car and passengers are brought to rest. Since force = rate of change of momentum, a larger stopping time means a smaller force on the occupants (here it falls from 40000 N to 10000 N), greatly reducing injury.
questions.explanation: Same change in momentum; longer time -> smaller force.
